concepts.title: Conditionals: if/else and switch
concepts.description: if/else chains pick exactly one branch by evaluating conditions top to bottom until the first true one wins, while switch jumps to the label matching a single value. Two Java rules trip up beginners here: classic switch cases fall through without a break, and conditions must be boolean.
learningObjectives: Write if/else if/else chains and explain the exact order Java evaluates them in, including which branches get skipped once a match is found.
Explain why Java requires a genuine boolean expression in an if condition, unlike languages with 'truthy' values, and what class of bug that prevents.
Use a classic switch statement correctly, including explaining fall-through behavior and why break is usually required.
Use a modern switch expression with arrow syntax and explain how it avoids fall-through by design.
Predict bugs caused by missing break statements in a switch and by ambiguous nested if/else without braces.

sections.heading: if / else if / else: Top to Bottom, First Match Wins
Conditions Must Be boolean
sections.body:
In C, `if (x)` is legal for an int x, and it's treated as true whenever x is nonzero. Many scripting languages generalize this further with 'truthy' and 'falsy' values for all sorts of types. Java does none of this. The expression inside an if must be a `boolean` (or a `Boolean`, which is unboxed and throws `NullPointerException` if it's null). `if (x)` where x is an int is a compile-time error, `incompatible types: int cannot be converted to boolean`.

This closes off a famous C bug. In C, `if (x = 5)` compiles: it's an assignment expression, x is set to 5, and the expression's value (5, nonzero) is treated as true, so the branch always runs, even though the programmer almost certainly meant `==` and intended a comparison. In Java, if x is an int, the exact same typo, `if (x = 5)`, fails to compile, because the type of an assignment expression is the type of the value assigned (here, int) and int is not a legal if-condition type. The compiler catches the typo before the program ever runs.

The protection has one gap. If `flag` is itself a `boolean`, `if (flag = true)` compiles, overwrites flag with true, and always takes the branch. Avoid it by never comparing a boolean to a literal: write `if (flag)` or `if (!flag)`.

sections.heading: Classic switch Statements and Fall-Through
switch Expressions and Arrow Syntax

examples.title: The Fall-Through Bug in a Classic switch
examples.explanation: day matches case 3, so execution jumps straight to the "Wednesday" println, but none of case 3, case 4, or default has a break statement, so control keeps falling straight through each subsequent case's code regardless of whether its label matches anything. The result is that this prints three lines (Wednesday, Thursday, Some other day) when a reader skimming the case 3 label alone would reasonably expect only one. By default javac gives no warning, so the bug only shows up when you run the code and read the output.

examples.title: Fixed with break, and the Modern Arrow Alternative
examples.explanation: In the classic form, adding break after each case's println stops execution from continuing into the next case the moment a match's code has finished: day == 3 now prints only "Wednesday", exactly once, matching what a reader would naturally expect from the label alone. The arrow-based switch expression achieves the same correct result through a completely different mechanism: rather than relying on break to opt out of a default fall-through behavior, each case -> value branch is self-contained and independent by construction, so there's no shared control-flow path between cases for execution to accidentally fall into. Both versions here produce identical output for day == 3, but the arrow form makes the missing-break class of bug impossible rather than merely avoided by discipline.

examples.title: if (x) Doesn't Compile for a Non-boolean x
examples.explanation: The commented-out block would fail to compile, because Java's if statement requires its condition to already be a boolean expression: there is no implicit 'nonzero counts as true' conversion the way there is in C or many scripting languages. Writing the comparison out, x != 0, produces a boolean, which is what if always requires. This restriction is a direct, practical benefit of static typing: an entire class of typo bugs (writing = where you meant ==, in languages that would otherwise accept a numeric condition) cannot compile in Java when the variable involved is a non-boolean type.

misconceptions.description: In a switch statement, only the matching case's code runs and then execution automatically stops there, the same way an if/else if chain stops after its first matching branch.
misconceptions.clarification: switch and if/else if behave differently here, and conflating them is how fall-through bugs happen. An if/else if chain inherently runs at most one branch, by its own structure: there's no way for two branches to both execute. A classic switch, by contrast, finds the matching case label and then keeps executing every line after it, across every subsequent case, until it hits a break (or the switch ends). Matching a label is only where execution starts, not where it's guaranteed to stop. The modern arrow-based switch expression restores the 'only one branch runs' behavior beginners expect from the classic form, but it does so by design, not by adding an implicit stop: there's no shared path for execution to fall through along.

misconceptions.description: Java's requirement that if conditions be a genuine boolean makes the classic C bug of writing = instead of == in a condition completely impossible in Java.
misconceptions.clarification: It closes the bug for numeric and object types, but not universally. if (x = 5) fails to compile when x is an int, because the assignment expression's type (int) isn't a legal condition type, this is the protection working as intended. But if flag is already declared as a boolean, if (flag = true) compiles without complaint, because the assigned value's type is boolean, which is what if requires; it reassigns flag to true and always takes the branch, which is the identical bug, just relocated to the one case where the types happen to line up. The rule to take away is: Java's type system prevents this bug whenever the variable's type isn't boolean, not whenever the variable is being used in a boolean context.

exercises.prompt: What does this print, and why?
hints: Find which case label matches month == 2 first, then check: does that specific case end with a break?
If a case has no break, execution keeps running the code for every case AFTER it too, regardless of whether those labels match anything.
Trace forward from case 2 until you hit the first break you encounter: everything printed along the way is part of the output.
exercises.expectedAnswer:
February
March
Because case 2 has no break, execution falls through into case 3's code and stops there, since case 3 does have a break.
exercises.solutionExplanation: month == 2 matches case 2, which prints "February", but case 2 has no break statement, so control falls straight through into case 3's code next, printing "March" as well. case 3 does have a break, so execution stops there, and case 4 and default are never reached. The output is therefore two lines, February and March, even though only one case label matched the value 2.

exercises.prompt: This method is supposed to print exactly one line describing a traffic light color, but for "yellow" it prints two lines instead of one. Find and fix the bug.
hints: Look at the case "yellow" block: does it end with a break before moving on to the next case?
Without a break, control keeps executing into case "green"'s code too, even though the color passed in was never "green".
Add the missing break right after the 'yellow' case's println, the same way 'red' and 'green' already have one.
exercises.solutionExplanation: The case "yellow" block prints "Slow down" but has no break, so execution falls straight through into case "green"'s code next, printing "Go" as well, even though the argument passed in was "yellow", never "green". Adding break right after the "yellow" case's println stops execution there, matching the pattern already correctly used for "red" and "green". A missing break causes no exception and, by default, no compiler warning, only extra output that is easy to overlook.

options: This fails to compile because case 1 has no break.
one

one
two
three

one
two
assessments.explanation: n matches case 1 and prints "one", but case 1 has no break, so execution falls through into case 2's code next, printing "two" as well; case 2 does have a break, so execution stops there and case 3 is never reached, giving exactly two lines: one, then two. The “one” option wrongly assumes execution stops automatically after a match, the way if/else if does. The “one two three” option wrongly assumes it keeps falling through past case 2's break. The “This fails to compile because case 1…” option is wrong because a case without a break is completely legal Java.

assessments.prompt: Explain, to a beginner who is confused about why their switch statement is printing more than they expected, what fall-through is, why the language behaves this way, and how the modern switch expression avoids the problem entirely.
assessments.modelAnswer: In a classic Java switch statement, matching a case label is only where execution starts; it is not, by itself, where execution stops. Once control jumps to the matching case, it keeps running every subsequent line of code, straight through the boundaries of the next case labels too, completely ignoring whether those later labels match the switched-on value at all, until it either hits a break statement or reaches the very end of the switch block. This is called fall-through, and it's the reason a switch can end up printing output from cases that were never matched: if you forget a break at the end of a matched case's code, you get that case's output plus whatever comes immediately after it too, with no runtime error and no compiler warning unless you enable -Xlint:fallthrough. Java inherited the behavior from C, and it has one use: several case labels can share one block of code by being stacked with no statements between them. In most switch statements, though, each case is meant to be independent, and a forgotten break is an easy-to-miss bug. Java 14 introduced switch expressions using arrow syntax (case value -> result) to avoid this: each arm is a self-contained branch that produces a value, so there's nothing to fall through into and no break to forget.

assessments.prompt: int a = -5; int b = 10; if (a > 0) if (b > 0) System.out.println("both positive"); else System.out.println("not both positive"); What does this print?
options: This fails to compile, because the else here is ambiguous without braces.
not both positive, because a > 0 is false, so the else branch handles that case.
Nothing at all -- Java always attaches an else to the nearest unmatched if.
both positive, because a > 0 is false, which Java treats as satisfying the outer if for this construct.
assessments.explanation: The compiler always binds a dangling else to the nearest if that doesn't already have one, regardless of indentation; here, that's if (b > 0), not if (a > 0). So the code means: if (a > 0) { if (b > 0) print both positive; else print not both positive; }. With a = -5, the outer if (a > 0) is false, so its entire body (the whole nested if/else) is skipped as a single unit, and nothing prints at all. The “not both positive, because a > 0…” option comes from pairing the else with the outer if, but layout and intent have no effect on how else binds. The “This fails to compile, because the else…” option is wrong because this is legal, unambiguous (to the compiler) Java, even without braces. The “both positive, because a > 0…” option describes behavior Java doesn't have.

assessments.prompt: boolean flag = false; if (flag = true) { System.out.println("branch taken"); } System.out.println(flag); What does this print, and why does it compile at all, given that Java requires genuine boolean conditions?
options: It prints only false, because flag = true inside an if condition is interpreted as a comparison, not an assignment.

branch taken, then true -- flag = true is itself an assignment expression whose resulting value is the boolean true (the value just assigned), which is a perfectly legal if condition; the branch runs, and flag is left reassigned to true as a side effect.
This fails to compile, because = is never a valid operator to use inside an if condition.
This throws a runtime exception, because assignment expressions cannot be evaluated as part of a condition.
assessments.explanation: An assignment expression's type is the type of the value assigned (here, boolean, since true is a boolean literal) and boolean is what if requires, so this compiles without complaint. The if condition therefore evaluates to true (the just-assigned value), the branch runs and prints branch taken, and flag itself has been reassigned to true as a side effect of evaluating the condition, which the final println then confirms. Java's protection against the = vs == typo only applies when the variable's type isn't boolean. The “This fails to compile, because =…” option is wrong because assignment expressions are legal wherever an expression of the required type is allowed. The “This throws a runtime exception, because assignment…” option is wrong because there's nothing runtime-exceptional about evaluating an assignment inside a condition. The “It prints only false, because flag =…” option is wrong because = is assignment, not comparison, in Java under any circumstance.

assessments.prompt: String result = switch (grade) { case 'A' -> "Excellent"; case 'B' -> "Good"; default -> { String fallback = "Needs improvement"; yield fallback; } }; What does yield do in that default branch, and could break be used there instead?
options: yield hands back the value that branch's block contributes to the overall switch expression's result; break cannot be used there.
yield and break are fully interchangeable in every form of switch, including this arrow-based expression form.
yield discards the block's computed value and forces the switch expression to fall through into whatever case is written after default.
yield is only legal inside a default branch -- every other case in a switch expression is required to omit braces entirely.
assessments.explanation: When a case in a switch expression needs more than one expression's worth of logic, a braced block can compute intermediate values and then hand back the branch's overall result with yield; here it hands back fallback. break ends a switch statement without producing a value, and the compiler rejects any attempt to break out of a switch expression. The “yield and break are fully interchangeable…” option is wrong because break produces no value, while a switch expression must. The “yield is only legal inside a default…” option is wrong: any case, not just default, may use a braced block with yield when it needs more than a single expression. The “yield discards the block's computed value…” option misdescribes yield; it produces a value, it doesn't discard one, and switch expressions have no fall-through to force in the first place.

concepts.title: Loops: for, while, and do-while
concepts.description: Java's three loop forms differ in when the condition is checked and how the iteration variable is managed. break, continue, and labels control which iteration, or which loop, gets interrupted.
learningObjectives: Trace the exact execution order of a for loop's init, condition, and update clauses across multiple iterations.
Choose between for, while, and do-while based on whether the iteration count is known ahead of time and whether the body must run at least once.
Explain precisely when do-while checks its condition relative to when while checks its, and what that changes in practice.
Use break and continue correctly, including labeled break/continue for escaping or skipping in nested loops.
Predict and diagnose an infinite loop caused by a missing or incorrect update step.
Use the enhanced for-each loop over arrays, and explain why it cannot be used to reassign an element back into a primitive array.

sections.heading: The for Loop: init, condition, update
while and do-while: Checking Before vs Checking After
break, continue, and Labeled Loops
The for-each Loop and Its Limits
How Infinite Loops Happen

examples.title: Tracing a for Loop's Exact Execution Order
examples.explanation: int i = 0 runs exactly once, before anything else. Then the sequence is: check i < 3 (true, since i is 0) -> run body, printing 'i = 0' -> run i++ , making i 1 -> check i < 3 again (true) -> print 'i = 1' -> i++ makes i 2 -> check (true) -> print 'i = 2' -> i++ makes i 3 -> check i < 3 (now false) -> loop ends without running the body again. So exactly three lines print, for i = 0, 1, and 2. I = 3 is checked but never printed, because the condition is evaluated before the body runs on every pass, including what would have been the fourth one.

examples.title: do-while Guarantees the Body Runs at Least Once
examples.explanation: This simulates a retry-until-valid pattern: attempt 1 and attempt 2 produce -1 (treated as invalid), so the do-while condition result < 0 keeps the loop going; attempt 3 finally produces 42, and the condition becomes false, ending the loop right after that iteration's body has already run. The key point is that result does not exist with any meaningful value before the first iteration: there's nothing to check yet, so do-while's 'run the body first, check after' order matches this pattern. A plain while loop attempting the same logic would need some way to get an initial result before the loop even starts, just to have something to test against the first condition check, typically forcing you to duplicate the body's first line above the loop.

examples.title: Labeled break to Escape Nested Loops in One Step
examples.explanation: value equals target (5) when row is 1 and col is 2 (1*3 + 2 = 5). break search; exits both the inner and outer for loops in that single statement, because search is a label attached to the outer loop: execution jumps straight to the println after the nested loops, never checking row 2 at all, since there's no point once the target has already been found. Without the label, an unlabeled break here would only exit the inner loop; the outer loop would then proceed to row = 2 and needlessly run through all of its columns too, even though found is already true.

misconceptions.description: continue works like a weaker version of break -- it still ends the loop, just somehow less abruptly.
misconceptions.clarification: continue does not end the loop at all. It skips only the remainder of the current iteration's body and jumps straight to the next iteration's condition check (running the update step first, in a for loop); the loop keeps running as it otherwise would, for as many remaining iterations as its condition allows. break, by contrast, terminates the loop immediately and completely, with no further iterations of any kind.

misconceptions.description: In a for-each loop like for (int x : numbers), assigning a new value to x inside the loop body updates the corresponding element back in the numbers array.
misconceptions.clarification: For an array of primitive elements, x is a copy of each element, freshly created for that iteration. It has no ongoing connection back to the array's storage. Reassigning x only changes that local copy, and the array itself is completely unaffected once the loop moves to the next iteration. To mutate elements in place, you need the classic indexed for loop and an assignment through the array itself, such as numbers[i] = newValue, which writes into the array's own storage rather than into a throwaway per-iteration copy.
misconceptions.fact: For an array of primitive elements, x is a copy of each element, freshly created for that iteration. It has no ongoing connection back to the array's storage.

exercises.prompt: What does this print, and why?
hints: continue at i == 2 skips only the println for that one iteration: does the loop keep going afterward, or does it stop?
break at i == 4 is a completely different action from continue: what does it do to the rest of the loop's remaining iterations?
List out i's values in order (0,1,2,3,4) and decide, for each one, whether it reaches the println at all.
exercises.expectedAnswer:
0
1
3
i=2 hits continue and skips its println only, i=3 prints normally, and i=4 hits break and stops the loop before its println ever runs.
exercises.solutionExplanation: For i = 0 and i = 1, neither if triggers, so both print normally. For i = 2, the continue statement runs, which skips only the println below it for this one iteration and jumps straight to the loop's update step (i++) and next condition check; the loop itself keeps going. For i = 3, again neither if triggers, so it prints normally. For i = 4, the break statement runs, which terminates the loop immediately and completely: its println never executes, and no further iterations happen at all (i = 5 is never reached, since the loop has already ended). The final output is therefore 0, 1, 3: three lines, with 2 skipped by continue and 4 (and anything beyond it) cut off by break.

exercises.prompt: This loop is supposed to print the numbers 5 down to 1, but it counts up from 5 and keeps printing with no end in sight. Find and fix the bug.
hints: For the loop to eventually stop, i > 0 has to become false at some point. What direction does i need to move for that to happen?
Look at the update step inside the loop body: what operation is it performing on i, and does that operation move i toward or away from satisfying i > 0 being false?
The loop needs i to count DOWN toward and past 0, not up away from it.
exercises.solutionExplanation: The condition i > 0 can only ever become false if i eventually reaches 0 or goes negative, but the original code uses i++, which increments i further away from zero on every iteration, so i > 0 stays true until i overflows past Integer.MAX_VALUE, more than two billion lines later. Changing i++ to i--, so i counts down instead of up, means i decreases by one each pass (5, 4, 3, 2, 1), and once i reaches 0, the condition i > 0 finally evaluates to false and the loop ends, after printing 5, 4, 3, 2, 1.

assessments.prompt: What is the key behavioral difference between while and do-while?
options: while checks its condition before running the body on every pass, including the first.
There is no real difference -- they are two equivalent ways of writing the same loop.
do-while automatically breaks out after exactly one iteration, while while can run any number of times.
do-while can only be used with integers, while while works with any type.
assessments.explanation: The difference is WHEN the condition is checked relative to the body: before every iteration for while (so a false condition up front means zero iterations), versus after the body for do-while (so the body is guaranteed to run at least once regardless of the condition's initial value). The “do-while can only be used with integers…” option is fabricated; neither loop is restricted to integers. The “do-while automatically breaks out after exactly one…” option is wrong: do-while can run any number of iterations, just like while; it only guarantees a minimum of one. The “There is no real difference -- they…” option is wrong because the order of the check decides whether the body can run zero times.

assessments.prompt: Explain the difference between break and continue, and then explain what a labeled break adds on top of an ordinary, unlabeled one.
assessments.modelAnswer: break and continue do different things to a loop. break terminates the nearest enclosing loop immediately: once it runs, no further iterations of that loop happen at all, and execution resumes at the first statement after the loop. continue is much narrower: it only skips whatever remains of the CURRENT iteration's body, then proceeds to the next iteration as normal. In a for loop, that means the update step still runs and the condition is still checked again, so the loop keeps going as it otherwise would for its remaining iterations. A labeled break addresses a specific limitation of the plain, unlabeled version: an ordinary break, written inside a loop that's nested inside another loop, only escapes the innermost loop it's inside of; the outer loop keeps running its remaining iterations untouched. By placing a label immediately before the outer loop and writing break outerLabel; inside the inner loop, you can exit both loops in one single statement, which is especially useful once you've found what you were looking for in a nested search and there's no reason to keep checking any further, in either loop. Labeled continue exists too, with the analogous meaning: skip the rest of the current iteration of the labeled (outer) loop, rather than just the loop the continue statement happens to be textually inside of.

assessments.prompt: int[] values = {1, 2, 3}; for (int v : values) { v = v * 10; } System.out.println(values[0]); What prints, and why?
options: 10, because v = v * 10 writes the multiplied value back into the array through the loop variable.
30, because whichever iteration reassigns v last is the one that ends up overwriting values[0].
This fails to compile, because a for-each loop's variable cannot be reassigned inside the loop body.
1, because v is a fresh copy of each element for that iteration; reassigning v has no connection back to the array's actual storage, so values itself is completely unchanged.
assessments.explanation: In a for-each loop over an array of primitives, v holds a copy of each element for that one iteration, with no ongoing connection back to the array's own storage. Reassigning v only changes that local copy; it never writes through to values, so values[0] is still 1 after the loop finishes, completely untouched by any of the three reassignments that happened inside the loop body. The “10, because v = v * 10…” option describes the behavior of an indexed loop writing through values[i], not a for-each loop's per-iteration copy. The “This fails to compile, because a for-each…” option is wrong: reassigning the loop variable is legal Java, it's pointless for affecting the underlying array. The “30, because whichever iteration reassigns v last…” option invents a mechanism (a 'last iteration wins' write-back) that for-each loops don't have.

assessments.prompt: outer: for (int i = 0; i < 3; i++) { for (int j = 0; j < 3; j++) { if (j == 1) { continue outer; } System.out.println(i + "," + j); } } What does this print?
options: 0,0 -- continue outer immediately terminates both the inner and outer loop the first time j == 1 is reached.

0,0
1,0
2,0 -- continue outer skips the rest of the inner loop's current pass and jumps straight to the outer loop's next iteration, restarting the inner loop from j = 0 each time.

0,0
0,1
0,2
1,0
1,1
1,2
2,0
2,1
2,2 -- continue outer has no actual effect on which pairs get printed.
This fails to compile, because continue cannot reference a label attached to an outer for loop.
assessments.explanation: For each value of i, the inner loop prints i,0 (j = 0), then hits j == 1 and runs continue outer, which skips the rest of that inner-loop pass and jumps straight to the outer loop's next iteration, running i++ and rechecking i < 3, rather than merely moving to the inner loop's next j. Because control leaves the inner loop before j ever reaches 2, and the inner loop restarts fresh at j = 0 for the next i, the output is exactly one line per outer iteration: 0,0 then 1,0 then 2,0. The “0,0 0,1 0,2 1,0 1,1 1,2 2,0…” option describes what would happen with no continue at all. The “0,0 -- continue outer immediately terminates both…” option confuses continue with break: continue never terminates a loop, it only skips ahead within it (to the outer loop's next pass, in the labeled case). The “This fails to compile, because continue cannot…” option is wrong because labeled continue targeting an outer loop is standard, legal Java.

assessments.prompt: for (int i = 10; i > 0; i++) { System.out.println(i); } What happens when this runs?
options: It prints nothing at all, because i > 0 is already false the moment i is initialized to 10.
It fails to compile, because a for loop's update clause must move the loop variable toward the condition eventually becoming false.
It keeps printing larger numbers, effectively without end, until int overflow makes i negative after about 2.1 billion passes.
It prints 10 down to 1 and then stops, since the loop is clearly intended to count down.
assessments.explanation: The update step moves i away from zero while the loop waits for i > 0 to become false, so it prints 10, 11, 12, 13 and so on. For practical purposes that's an infinite loop. It would end only when i++ overflows from Integer.MAX_VALUE to Integer.MIN_VALUE, a negative number, which takes more than two billion passes. The “It prints 10 down to 1…” option assumes the update direction matches the apparent intent of the code, but the compiler only executes what's written, not what was probably meant. The “It fails to compile…” option is wrong because Java's compiler has no way to verify, and no requirement, that a for loop's update clause is compatible with ever terminating. The “It prints nothing at all, because i…” option is wrong because i > 0 is true when i is 10, so the body does run, repeatedly.

concepts.title: Methods, Overloading, and Arrays
concepts.description: A method must honor its return type on every path through its body. Overloading lets methods share a name if their parameter lists differ, with the choice made at compile time. Arrays are fixed-size reference types, and passing one copies the reference, which decides which changes survive back in the caller.
learningObjectives: Define a method with an explicit return type and explain why every reachable path through a non-void method's body must return a value.
Define overloaded methods and explain how the compiler chooses which overload to call, based on the static types of the arguments at compile time.
Predict overload-resolution behavior involving primitive widening, explaining why it's attempted before autoboxing.
Declare, initialize, and index arrays, and explain why their size is fixed once created.
Explain what is actually copied when an array is passed to a method, and why mutation through that reference is visible to the caller while reassignment of the parameter is not.
Predict and explain ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException and NullPointerException scenarios involving arrays.

sections.heading: Methods and Return Types
Overloading: Same Name, Different Parameters
Overload Resolution Order: Exact Match, Then Widening, Then Autoboxing
sections.body:
When more than one overload could accept a call, Java follows a fixed order. For primitive arguments it works out like this: an overload matching the argument types **exactly** wins. Failing that, the compiler tries **widening** to a larger primitive type (`int` to `long`, `long` to `double`, and so on). Only then does it consider **autoboxing** (wrapping a primitive in its object wrapper, like `int` into `Integer`), and varargs parameters come last.

```java
static void show(long value) { System.out.println("long: " + value); }
static void show(Integer value) { System.out.println("Integer: " + value); }

show(5);   // prints "long: 5" -- widening int -> long wins over autoboxing int -> Integer
```

This surprises people who expect `Integer` because `5` 'is an int'. The reason is compatibility: autoboxing arrived in Java 5, and if it had been considered together with widening, existing code calling `show(long)` with an `int` could have started calling a different method after an upgrade. If neither an exact match, a widening conversion, nor autoboxing produces a single unambiguous best overload, the compiler reports an ambiguity error rather than guessing.

sections.heading: Arrays: Fixed-Size, Zero-Indexed, Reference-Type Containers
Passing Arrays to Methods: What's Actually Copied

examples.title: Overload Resolution at Compile Time
examples.explanation: There are three separate methods here, all named add, distinguished only by their parameter types. When the compiler sees add(2, 3), it looks at the static types of the arguments (two int literals) and picks the (int, int) overload, since that's an exact match; no widening or boxing is even needed. add(2.5, 3.5) similarly matches the (double, double) overload exactly, and add("2", "3") matches the (String, String) overload. Note this last one performs string concatenation, not numeric addition, because that's what + means for the String overload's body, unrelated to what + does in the other two. All of this is decided while javac is compiling the code, purely by looking at the argument types written at each call site; none of it depends on any value that only exists while the program is running.

examples.title: Widening Beats Autoboxing in Overload Resolution
examples.explanation: 5 is an int literal, and neither overload matches int exactly, so the compiler moves on to its fallback rules, in a fixed order: widening conversions are considered before autoboxing. Widening int to long is a same-family primitive conversion and is tried first; it succeeds, so show(long) is chosen. Autoboxing int to Integer would also technically make show(Integer) callable, but it's only ever considered if no widening conversion could satisfy the call, which isn't the case here. This often surprises people who expect Integer to win because '5 is basically an int already', but widening is checked first.

examples.title: Arrays Are References: Mutation Survives a Method Call, Reassignment Doesn't
examples.explanation: mutate receives a copy of the reference stored in numbers, but that copy still points at the exact same array object, so writing to arr[0] inside mutate writes into the one and only array that exists, and main sees the change through its own numbers variable afterward. reassign also receives a copy of that same reference, but arr = new int[]{1, 2, 3} does something different: it makes reassign's own local arr variable point at a brand-new array, without touching what numbers points at back in main at all. Once reassign returns, that new array it created is discarded (nothing else refers to it), and numbers in main is exactly as it was after mutate ran.

misconceptions.description: Overloaded methods are chosen at run time based on the actual object passed in, the same way method overriding works.
misconceptions.clarification: Overload resolution happens at compile time, based on the static (declared) types of the arguments at each call site: javac decides which overloaded method's code a given call will run, and that decision is baked into the compiled bytecode before the program ever executes. This is a fundamentally different mechanism from overriding, where a subclass provides its own version of an inherited method, and the version that runs is chosen at run time based on the actual type of the object the method is called on, not on how the reference variable is declared. Overloading is sometimes called 'compile-time polymorphism' and overriding 'run-time polymorphism'.

misconceptions.description: Passing an array into a method passes a full copy of the array's contents, so changes made to it inside the method can never affect the caller's array.
misconceptions.clarification: Java passes a copy of the array's REFERENCE, not a copy of its contents. The copied reference still points at the exact same array object the caller has. Mutating an element through that reference inside the method (arr[i] = newValue) writes into the one shared array and is visible to the caller once the method returns. What does NOT survive is reassigning the parameter variable itself (arr = new int[]{...}): that only repoints the method's own local copy of the reference, leaving the caller's variable pointing at the original, unaffected array. The two operations, mutating through the reference versus reassigning the reference, have opposite visibility outcomes, and it's the difference between them (not a blanket 'arrays are always copied' or 'arrays are never copied' rule) that matters.
misconceptions.fact: Java passes a copy of the array's REFERENCE, not a copy of its contents; the copied reference still points at the exact same array object the caller has.

exercises.prompt: What does this program print, and why?
hints: addPoint mutates scores[0] through the array reference it was given; is that reference the same one main's scores variable holds?
resetScores assigns a brand-new array to its own parameter named scores; does that reassignment reach back and change what main's scores variable points to?
Separate 'writing through the reference' (arr[i] = ...) from 'rebinding the reference itself' (arr = new int[...]): they have very different visibility outside the method.
exercises.expectedAnswer: 60, then 60. addPoint mutates the shared array through its reference, so the change is visible in main. resetScores only reassigns its own local copy of the parameter to a new array; main's scores variable still points at the original array, unaffected.
exercises.solutionExplanation: addPoint receives a copy of the reference stored in main's scores, but that copy points at the same underlying array, so scores[0] = scores[0] + 10 mutates that one shared array, changing its first element from 50 to 60, which main's own scores[0] reflects immediately afterward: 60. resetScores also receives a copy of that reference, but scores = new int[scores.length] only repoints resetScores's own local parameter variable at a freshly created array full of zeros. It does not, and cannot, change what main's scores variable points to. So after resetScores returns, main's scores is exactly as it was left by addPoint: still pointing at the original array with 60 in its first slot, giving a second printed line of 60, not 0.

exercises.prompt: This method is supposed to print every element of an array, but it throws ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException. Find and fix the bug.
hints: For an array of length 3, what are the valid indices, and does values.length itself ever count as a valid index?
Compare the loop's continuation condition, i <= values.length, against the valid index range.
Change the comparison operator so the loop stops one iteration earlier than it currently does.
exercises.solutionExplanation: For an array of length 3, the valid indices are 0, 1, and 2; index 3 (equal to the array's length) is one past the last element and does not exist. The original condition, i <= values.length, allows i to reach 3, and values[3] on that final pass throws ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException, since there is no fourth element. Changing the condition to i < values.length stops the loop after i = 2, the last valid index, which is the correct, idiomatic bound for iterating an array by index. When you don't need the index, a for-each loop avoids the boundary check altogether.

options: This throws a NullPointerException, because arr is reassigned inside grow.
1, because grow only reassigns its own local copy of the array reference -- it never changes what data, back in main, points to.
7, because grow replaces the array data refers to with a new one.
0, because reassigning the parameter resets the original array's contents to their default values.
assessments.explanation: grow receives a copy of the reference stored in data, and arr = new int[]{7, 8, 9} only repoints THAT local copy at a brand-new array: it has no way to reach back and change what main's own data variable points to, since that would require modifying the caller's variable, which passing a copy of a reference does not allow. So data in main still points at the original array {1, 2, 3}, completely unaffected, and data[0] prints 1. The “7, because grow replaces the array data…” option describes what would happen if arrays were passed by reference to the variable itself (which Java does not do); the “This throws a NullPointerException, because arr…” option is wrong because nothing here produces a null reference; the “0, because reassigning the parameter resets…” option is wrong because the original array's contents are never touched at all, only a separate, new, and ultimately unused array is created and then discarded once grow returns.

assessments.prompt: Explain why an array passed into a method can have its elements changed by that method (visible to the caller afterward), while reassigning the array parameter itself inside that method has no effect on the caller at all. Base your answer on what is copied when an argument is passed.
assessments.modelAnswer: Java is always pass-by-value, but for a reference type like an array, the 'value' being copied into the method's parameter is the reference itself: essentially an address pointing to where the array lives on the heap, not the array's contents. That copied reference still points at the exact same array object the caller has, so there are, at that point, two separate variables (the caller's and the method's parameter) both pointing at one shared array. If the method writes to an element through its reference, such as arr[0] = 99, it is writing into that one shared array object, and since the caller's variable points at that same object, the caller observes the change immediately after the method returns; nothing needs to be 'passed back'; the caller was always looking at the same underlying data. Reassigning the parameter itself, such as arr = new int[]{1, 2, 3}, is a completely different operation: it changes what the method's own local copy of the reference points to, aiming it at a newly created array instead. That reassignment only affects the method's local variable. It cannot reach back and change what the caller's own variable points to, because the caller's variable is a separate copy of the original reference, never connected to the method's local variable beyond having started out pointing at the same object. So the general rule is: any change made THROUGH a reference (mutating the object it points to) is visible everywhere that reference is shared, but any change made TO the reference itself (making it point elsewhere) is purely local to whichever variable was reassigned.

assessments.prompt: static void report(long value) { System.out.println("long: " + value); } static void report(Integer value) { System.out.println("Integer: " + value); } report(42); What prints, and why?
options: long: 42, because Java's overload resolution tries widening conversions (int to long) before it ever considers autoboxing (int to Integer), and the widening conversion succeeds here.
Integer: 42, because Integer is considered a more specific match than the primitive type long.
This is ambiguous and fails to compile, because both overloads are equally applicable to an int argument.
Integer: 42, because 42 is fundamentally an int, and autoboxing is always preferred whenever both an autoboxing overload and a widening overload are available.
assessments.explanation: 42 is an int literal, and neither overload matches int exactly, so the compiler falls back to its fixed preference order: widening a primitive to a larger compatible primitive is attempted before autoboxing is even considered. Widening int to long succeeds, so report(long) is selected, and the output is long: 42. Autoboxing to Integer is never reached because a widening match already resolved the call. The “Integer: 42, because 42 is fundamentally…” option states the resolution order backwards; widening is preferred over autoboxing, not the reverse. The “This is ambiguous and fails to compile…” option is wrong because this call isn't ambiguous at all: exactly one overload is reachable via the preferred conversion path. The “Integer: 42, because Integer is considered…” option is wrong because specificity isn't the deciding factor here; the fixed conversion-preference order (exact match, then widening, then autoboxing) is.

assessments.prompt: static int classify(int score) { if (score >= 60) { return 1; } } What happens when this is compiled?
options: It compiles fine, but throws an exception at run time whenever score is below 60.
It compiles fine, because only void methods are actually required to return a value on every possible path.
It fails to compile with a "missing return statement" error.
It compiles fine, implicitly returning 0 for any score below 60.
assessments.explanation: A method declared to return int must return on every reachable path. Here, if score is less than 60, the if body is skipped and execution reaches the closing brace of the method with nothing returned, a, reachable path with no return statement, which javac rejects at compile time rather than letting it become a runtime surprise. The “It compiles fine, implicitly returning 0…” option describes behavior Java doesn't have; there's no implicit default return value for non-void methods. The “It compiles fine, but throws an exception…” option is wrong because this code never compiles in the first place, so it can never run to throw anything. The “It compiles fine, because only void methods…” option has the requirement backwards: void methods are the ones exempt from this rule.
